wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e111.summary: Opens the whole commentary with the edition's incipit praising Master William of Ockham and noting that the Prologue raises and resolves twelve questions (four principal and eight connected). It then poses the first question: whether it is possible for the wayfarer's intellect to have evident knowledge of theological truths.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e155.summary: First argument for no: evident knowledge of a theological truth requires distinct knowledge of the deity under its proper ratio. Indistinct knowledge, possible from purely natural means, would make theological truths naturally evident, which is false. But knowledge of God under the proper ratio of deity, the infinite and beatifying object, is beatific and impossible for a wayfarer.
claims: Evident theological knowledge requires distinct knowledge of the deity (argument).
Knowledge of deity under its proper ratio is beatific (argument).

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e186.summary: Second argument: theological truths would be evident either as self-evident, known once the terms are known, which would make them naturally known to anyone grasping the terms, or through better-known truths. Not through what is better known absolutely, since nothing is prior to 'God is three and one', there being no middle between God and the three persons. Nor through what is better known only to us, since nothing posterior can lead to evident knowledge of that prior truth.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e221.summary: Third argument: evident knowledge of theological truths is the most perfect possible knowledge of a truth, and if a wayfarer could have it, the blessed would have no more perfect knowledge of them than the wayfarer, which is false.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e235.summary: Argument to the contrary: whoever can determinately apprehend the terms of a per se necessary proposition can evidently know it, from its terms if it is first, or through the first if not. A wayfarer can determinately know, at least abstractively, the terms of 'God is three and one', so can evidently know it, and likewise other non-first theological truths.
claims: Whoever determinately apprehends the terms of a necessary per se proposition can evidently know it.
A wayfarer can abstractively know the terms of 'God is three and one'.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e264.summary: Plans to explain the question's terms: what 'the wayfarer's intellect' means, what 'evident knowledge' means, what 'theological truth' means, and then to answer the question.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e277.summary: Defines the wayfarer's intellect as one that does not have intuitive knowledge of the deity but for which it is possible by God's ordained power. The first part excludes the blessed, who have intuitive knowledge of deity. The second excludes the damned, for whom it is impossible by ordained power, though possible by absolute power.
claims: The wayfarer lacks intuitive knowledge of deity but can attain it by God's ordained power.
The damned can have intuitive knowledge of deity only by absolute power.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e295.summary: Defines evident knowledge: knowledge of a true complex apt to be sufficiently caused, mediately or immediately, by incomplex knowledge of terms, whether of that proposition or of others. It follows that evident knowledge is broader than science, understanding or wisdom, since a contingent proposition can be evidently known without being the object of any of Aristotle's habits in Ethics VI.
claims: Evident knowledge is knowledge of a true complex apt to be sufficiently caused by incomplex knowledge of terms.
Evident knowledge is broader than science, understanding or wisdom.
Contingent propositions can be evidently known.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e330.summary: Objection: knowledge of a contingent truth is never sufficiently caused by knowledge of incomplex terms, or it would be known from its terms and so be a first, self-evident principle (Posterior Analytics I). No contingent truth is self-evident.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e343.summary: Reply: a self-evident proposition is one known evidently from any knowledge of its terms, abstractive or intuitive. This is impossible for a contingent proposition, since some knowledge of the terms suffices for its evident knowledge (intuitive) and some does not (abstractive). Seeing Socrates and the whiteness in him intuitively, one evidently knows that Socrates is white. Knowing them only abstractively, as one can imagine them in their absence, one would not.
claims: A self-evident proposition is evidently known from any knowledge of its terms.
Intuitive knowledge of terms suffices for evident knowledge of contingent truths; abstractive knowledge does not.
Seeing Socrates' whiteness intuitively yields evident knowledge that Socrates is white.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e377.summary: Defines theological truths: all truths necessary for the wayfarer to attain eternal beatitude. Supported by Augustine (De Trinitate XIV.1), who assigns to this science not everything humanly knowable, which is full of vanity and harmful curiosity, but only what generates, nourishes, defends and strengthens saving faith.
claims: Theological truths are all truths necessary for the wayfarer's salvation.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e409.summary: It follows that some naturally known or knowable truths are theological, such as that God exists, is wise, is good, since these are necessary for salvation. Others are known supernaturally, such as that God is triune and incarnate.
claims: Some naturally knowable truths, like God's existence, are theological.
The Trinity and Incarnation are known only supernaturally.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e422.summary: Objection: every naturally knowable proposition belongs to some naturally discovered science, and the same truth does not belong to distinct sciences, so no naturally knowable truth is theological.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e435.summary: Further: a truth provable through a subject into which the predicate resolves as middle belongs to the science of that middle subject. 'God is wise', 'God is good' can be proved through being ('every being is good; God is a being'), so they belong to the science of being, not of God.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e455.summary: Confirmation: these are properties of being, so truths following from them belong only to the science of being, since one science considers a subject and its properties.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e471.summary: Further: according to Posterior Analytics I one may not pass from genus to genus in demonstrating, but if the same truth belonged to distinct sciences, one science's principles would prove another's conclusions.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e485.summary: Answers the first objection: 'science' has two senses. In one, it is a collection of many items ordered to knowledge of one or many things. It contains incomplex knowledge of terms, complex knowledge of principles and conclusions, refutations of errors and false arguments, divisions and definitions, and the divisive, definitive and collative modes of proceeding. It is the sense used for the compilations of authors, as when the Physics or Posterior Analytics speaks of a science, or one says the Metaphysics is one science. Such a science is not numerically one but contains many habits differing in species and often in genus, unified by a special order. In this sense the same truth can belong to distinct sciences, even naturally discovered ones, since one conclusion can be evidently proved by different middles. A truth can be a principle in one and a conclusion in another, especially when the subject of one is contained under the subject of another, as God (the theologian's subject) under being (the metaphysician's). Averroes says the physicist proves separate substances exist and the metaphysician presupposes it, and some hold God's existence is proved in metaphysics as well as theology. Even if not, the same truth can belong to a strict science and to a 'science' broadly meaning firm adhesion, as theology largely is.
claims: 'Science' can mean an ordered collection of many habits.
In that sense the same truth can belong to distinct sciences.
A truth can be a principle in one science and a conclusion in another.
God, theology's subject, is contained under being, metaphysics' subject.
Theology is largely a science only in the sense of firm adhesion.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e600.summary: In the other sense, science is a habit in the genus of quality distinguished from understanding, wisdom, art and prudence. In this sense the same truth does not belong to distinct sciences, since each such science is numerically one thing for one conclusion. Against the objection that distinct demonstrations of the same conclusion cause distinct sciences: distinct premises do not always cause distinct sciences, just as heat of the same species can come from fire or sun.
claims: In the strict sense, one conclusion has only one science.
Distinct premises can cause the same species of science.
Fire and sun produce heat of the same species.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e692.summary: Answers the second objection: the same truth can belong to both sciences in the first sense. Against the inference that they would then be one science (like the science of the soul and of the intellective soul): they need not form one science unless both concerned precisely the subject of that truth and its duly ordered properties. If they consider many subjects and properties lacking the required order, as metaphysics and theology do, they are not one. To the confirmation: these are properties of being and so belong to metaphysics, but they can also belong to other sciences.
claims: The same truth can belong to two ordered collections without merging them.
Metaphysics and theology are not one science.
Properties of being belong to metaphysics but can belong to other sciences too.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e684.summary: Further, granting that truths proving properties of being of God belong only to metaphysics, all truths stating properties proper to God alone, virtually contained under the proper ratio of deity on the opponents' way of speaking, belong to the science of God under that ratio: 'God is triune', 'God is infinite', 'God is the first cause of all', 'God is pure act'.
claims: Truths stating properties proper to God belong to the science of God under the ratio of deity.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e715.summary: Against the reply that such properties are demonstrated of God in metaphysics and so do not belong to theology: in metaphysics they are demonstrated only quia, while in theology, on the opponents' own view, they are demonstrated propter quid of God under the proper ratio of deity and resolve ultimately into rationes of deity. If quia demonstration makes them metaphysical, propter quid demonstration all the more makes them theological.
claims: Metaphysics demonstrates divine properties only quia; theology (on the opponents' view) propter quid.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e744.summary: Objection: then one and the same habit would be both metaphysical and theological.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e752.summary: Reply: taking the metaphysical and theological habit as commonly understood, neither is numerically one but contains many habits differing in number, species and genus. So the habit by which one knows 'God is one', belonging to both metaphysics and theology, is neither metaphysical nor theological, just as a man is not an army or people, nor a house a city. If 'metaphysical' or 'theological' means belonging to metaphysics or theology, then the same habit is both, being part of each, as a man is part of a people and of an army.
claims: Metaphysics and theology are aggregates of many habits.
A single habit can be part of both metaphysics and theology.
A part of an aggregate is not itself the aggregate.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e791.summary: Answers the third objection: Aristotle speaks of sciences with wholly distinct subjects and properties, and for those the principles of one cannot demonstrate the conclusions of another. When one science's subject is contained under another's, it can be done, as Aristotle there exempts such sciences. Here God, a partial subject of theology, is contained under being, the subject of another science.
claims: The prohibition on crossing genera applies only to sciences with wholly distinct subjects.
God, a partial subject of theology, is contained under being.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e824.summary: Against the reply that Aristotle exempts only subalternating and subalternated sciences: by exempting those he means to exempt others otherwise subordinated, though he does not say so. It is not unfitting for part of theology to be subalternated to metaphysics or the reverse, as part of medicine is subalternated to geometry (Posterior Analytics I).
claims: Part of theology may be subalternated to metaphysics or the reverse.
Part of medicine is subalternated to geometry.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e848.summary: Clarifies the scope of the question: it concerns evident knowledge in general, not scientific evident knowledge, since some supernaturally knowable theological truths are necessary and some contingent, and the contingent ones cannot be known scientifically either naturally or supernaturally. It concerns precisely supernaturally knowable truths, necessary or contingent.
claims: The question concerns evident knowledge in general of supernaturally knowable truths.
Contingent theological truths cannot be scientifically known.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e870.summary: Sets out the plan. First, Ockham will show that our intellect, even in this state, can have two specifically distinct incomplex cognitions of the same object under the same ratio, one intuitive and the other abstractive.
claims: Our intellect can have specifically distinct intuitive and abstractive cognitions of the same object.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e883.summary: Second, that such a twofold cognition of God under the proper ratio of deity is possible.
claims: Both intuitive and abstractive cognition of God under the ratio of deity are possible.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e891.summary: Third, that each of these cognitions is separable from the other.
claims: Intuitive and abstractive cognition are mutually separable.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e896.summary: Fourth, from this he will conclude that abstractive cognition of the deity is possible for the wayfarer.
claims: Abstractive cognition of deity is possible for the wayfarer.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e903.summary: Fifth, he will answer the form of the question.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e908.summary: Sixth, he will raise and resolve some doubts.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e913.summary: To prove the first conclusion, he first sets out preliminary distinctions and conclusions. First distinction: there are two acts of the intellect. The apprehensive act concerns anything that can terminate the intellect's act, complex or incomplex, since we apprehend propositions and demonstrations, necessary and possible, as well as incomplexes.
claims: The apprehensive act concerns anything, complex or incomplex, that can terminate an intellectual act.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e937.summary: The other is the judicative act, by which the intellect not only apprehends but assents or dissents. It concerns only complexes, since we assent only to what we think true and dissent only from what we think false. So regarding a complex there are two acts, apprehensive and judicative.
claims: The judicative act is assent or dissent and concerns only complexes.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e956.summary: Proof: one can apprehend a proposition without assenting or dissenting, as with neutral propositions, or a layperson hearing Latin propositions without understanding. And the intellect can assent to one proposition and dissent from another.
claims: One can apprehend a proposition without judging it.
Neutral propositions are apprehended without assent or dissent.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e982.summary: Second distinction: corresponding to the two acts regarding a complex there are two habits, one inclining to apprehension and one to judgment. After many apprehensions of a neutral proposition one feels more inclined to think about it, so there is an apprehensive habit. Aristotle's understanding, science and so on (Ethics VI) show there are judicative habits.
claims: There are apprehensive and judicative habits corresponding to the two acts.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e1011.summary: First preliminary conclusion: a judicative act about a complex presupposes an apprehensive act about it. No habit inclines to another habit's act except through its own act (the habit of a principle inclines to knowing a conclusion only through the principle's act). The apprehensive habit inclines to the judicative act, so it first inclines to its own apprehensive act. The two acts coexist, and the apprehensive can exist without the judicative but not the reverse, so it is naturally prior. The minor is shown by experience: someone who has often thought about a neutral proposition and then assents feels readier to assent and think of it afterward than one assent alone would explain, so the readiness comes partly from the habit acquired by apprehensive acts.
claims: A judicative act presupposes an apprehensive act about the same complex.
No habit inclines to another habit's act except through its own act.
The apprehensive act is naturally prior to the judicative act.
Prior apprehensions make later assent easier.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e1072.summary: Objections: then two acts of understanding would be in the same intellect at once. Also, when one habit inclines to another's act, the first habit's act is a sufficient cause of the second's act (the principle's act suffices for knowing the conclusion). So whoever apprehended a proposition would at once assent or dissent, which is plainly false.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e1109.summary: Third objection: the proof fails, since someone who often thinks about a neutral proposition and then assents does so not by the apprehensive habit but by virtue of the principle, authority or reason for which they now assent. Without remembering those, they would be inclined only to think of it, not to assent.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e1140.summary: Answers the first: Ockham concedes that several acts of understanding exist at once in the same intellect, not only ordered acts like apprehension and judgment but disparate ones, as will be shown.
claims: Several acts of understanding, even disparate ones, can exist simultaneously in one intellect.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e1154.summary: Proves this generally: every act naturally posterior to an act of love is really distinct from an act naturally prior to it. Peter can love Socrates and know that he loves Socrates. The act of knowing 'Peter loves Socrates' is naturally posterior to the love, since the love can exist without it but not the reverse, and coexists with it. The love presupposes incomplex knowledge of Socrates and coexists with it. So three acts coexist, two in the intellect and the middle one in the will.
claims: Two acts of intellect can coexist with an act of will between them.
Knowledge of one's own love is posterior to and coexists with the love.
Love presupposes incomplex knowledge of its object.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e1185.summary: Answers the second by denying the major: it suffices that the first act be a partial cause. The habit of one premise, through its act, inclines to knowing the conclusion, yet that act is not a sufficient cause, only with the other premise's act. Generally it suffices to be a mediate, at least partial, cause.
claims: A habit's act need only be a partial cause of the act it inclines to.
Neither premise alone suffices for knowledge of the conclusion.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e1203.summary: Answers the third: someone with a habit from earlier acts later assents by virtue of the principle or authority, but only partially, since with equal relation to the principle or authority and no prior thought, they would not assent as easily or often as after an intense habit. Assenting 'by virtue of' something has two senses: as that thing being the cause of assent (in which sense one assents by virtue of the apprehensive act, as one assents by virtue of God, the efficient cause, or of the intellect on some views), or as that to which one assents more, in which sense one does not assent by virtue of an apprehensive act, though it may be an efficient cause. Second preliminary conclusion: every judicative act presupposes in the same power incomplex knowledge of the terms, since it presupposes an apprehensive act, which presupposes incomplex knowledge (Averroes, De anima III, comm. 21 and 22: the intellect first understands simples and then composes them, and the power apprehending simple and composite must be the same).
claims: Prior apprehensive habits partially cause later assent.
'Assenting by virtue of X' can mean X causes the assent or X is more assented to.
Every judicative act presupposes incomplex knowledge of terms in the same power.
The intellect first understands simples and then composes them.
concepts: same power for simple and complex

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e1299.summary: Third preliminary conclusion: no act of the sensitive part is the immediate and proximate cause, partial or total, of any judicative act of the intellect. Whatever suffices as proximate cause for one judicative act suffices for all, and for a conclusion what is in the intellect suffices: given knowledge of the premises, the conclusion is known with all else removed.
claims: No sensitive act is an immediate cause of an intellectual judgment.
Knowledge of premises in the intellect suffices for knowing the conclusion.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e1328.summary: Further: since causes in the intellective part suffice, positing other causes is superfluous.
claims: Superfluous causes should not be posited.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e1335.summary: Proves the first main conclusion: incomplex knowledge of terms that can cause evident knowledge of a proposition composed of them differs in species from incomplex knowledge of the same terms that, however intensified, cannot. Things of the same kind and perfection have effects of the same kind in an equally disposed patient (Topics VII). Experience shows the intellect can have incomplex knowledge of Socrates and whiteness by which it cannot evidently know whether he is white, and also intuitive knowledge by which it can, if he is white. So there are two incomplex cognitions of them, one able to cause evident knowledge of the contingent proposition and the other not, and they differ in species.
claims: Incomplex cognitions that can and cannot cause evident knowledge of a contingent proposition differ in species.
Equal causes of the same kind have like effects in like patients.
There are intuitive and abstractive incomplex cognitions of the same things.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e1384.summary: Confirmation from Aristotle: we do not know sensibles when they are outside sense (Posterior Analytics), and contingents outside sense are hidden as to whether they exist (Ethics VI.3). So of a sensible, even in this state, there is an incomplex knowledge by which one can evidently know whether it exists, and another, when it is outside sense, by which one cannot.
claims: Sensibles outside sense are not known to exist.
Of a sensible there is both a cognition yielding knowledge of its existence and one that does not.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e1413.summary: Objection: incomplex knowledge of the terms does not suffice for evident knowledge of the contingent truth; some further knowledge is required.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e1420.summary: Reply: 'whiteness exists' depends on no knowledge except that by which I know it. Such knowledge is necessary or contingent. Not necessary, since a contingent truth does not follow from a necessary one. Not contingent, since then the same question arises, leading to infinite regress unless it rests on incomplex knowledge of terms. So for some contingent truth incomplex knowledge alone suffices, yet one can have incomplex knowledge of the same things and not know the truth. So there are two specifically distinct incomplex cognitions.
claims: A contingent truth does not follow from a necessary one.
Some contingent truths are known evidently from incomplex knowledge alone.
Regress of contingent truths must terminate in incomplex knowledge.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e1451.summary: Objection: the proof shows only that we can have two such cognitions of the terms, not that both are intellectual. It suffices that one be sensitive, by which the contingent truth is known, and the other intellectual, by which it is not. When the terms are sensed the truth is evident, and when only imagined or understood it is not. The authorities speak of this pair, one by exterior sense and one by intellect or imagination. Aristotle (Metaphysics VI) and the Commentator agree that singulars are not manifest when they leave sense: only an impression remains and no certainty of existence, and contingents are judged to exist when seen as present (Ethics VI comm. 24). So sensibles become manifest as to contingent truth through sense alone.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e1521.summary: Reply: sensitive intuitive knowledge does not suffice for knowledge of a contingent truth. Intellectual intuitive knowledge must also be posited. The intellect, having incomplex knowledge of the extremes, assents when they are sensed and not otherwise, so it must have a different incomplex knowledge of them when sensed. As forming a proposition in the intellect presupposes incomplex knowledge of terms in the intellect, evident knowledge presupposes intuitive knowledge in the intellect, not only in sense. No sensitive act is a proximate cause of judgment, so the intellect must have some new knowledge preceding the judgment. Averroes (De anima III comm. 22) confirms that the intellect understands singulars with their times and judges that things will be or were, so intellectual intuition suffices as proximate cause of judgment, and the intellect knows singulars as sense does.
claims: Sensitive intuition alone does not suffice for evident knowledge of contingent truths.
There is intellectual intuitive cognition of sensible singulars.
The intellect knows singulars and their times.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e1602.summary: This answers the authorities: contingent truths about sensibles can be known only when they are under sense, because in this state intellectual intuition of bodies cannot be had without sensitive intuition. So sensitive intuition is not superfluous, though intellectual intuition alone would suffice if it could naturally exist without sensation, as in angels and the separated soul.
claims: In this state intellectual intuition of bodies requires sensitive intuition.
In angels and separated souls intellectual intuition suffices without sense.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e1627.summary: Objection: intellectual intuition is not destroyed when a sensitive act ceases, so a contingent truth about a sensible could be evident without sensing it. Reply: just as the intellect can cease from all acts upon a bodily change such as illness or sleep, intellectual intuition can cease when external sensation ceases.
claims: Intellectual intuition of a sensible can cease when sensation ceases.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e1656.summary: Second main argument: any purely intelligible object, of which some incomplex knowledge suffices for evident contingent knowledge and some does not, can be known by two specifically distinct cognitions. Affections, intellections, pleasures and sorrows are purely intelligible and in no way sensible, and both kinds of knowledge are possible of them. Everyone experiences that they understand, love, delight, grieve. This contingent knowledge cannot come from necessary propositions, so it comes from incomplex knowledge of terms or from contingent complex knowledge, on pain of infinite regress. No proposition about a sensible entails that delight is in the will, so it must come from incomplex knowledge of purely intelligible terms. And one can know such an intelligible incomplexly yet not know whether it exists, as with another's delight seen once and later thought of.
claims: Acts of understanding, love, delight and sorrow are purely intelligible and not sensible.
Everyone experiences their own mental acts.
No proposition about sensibles entails that delight is in the will.
Knowledge of one's own mental acts rests on incomplex intuitive cognition of them.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e1741.summary: This argument shows the twofold cognition is possible for purely intelligible objects, while the first shows we actually have it for sensibles in this state. It is confirmed by Augustine (De Trinitate XIII.1): each sees faith in his own heart, if he believes, otherwise than bodies are seen or imagined. Faith, belonging to no bodily sense, can be known by a cognition sufficient for judging that it exists and by one that is not.
claims: The twofold cognition is possible for purely intelligible objects.
One sees one's own faith in a way different from bodies.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e1782.summary: Concludes the first article: of an incomplex there is a twofold cognition, one intuitive and the other abstractive. Ockham does not care whether others call it intuitive; his main point is that the intellect can have two specifically distinct incomplex cognitions of the same thing.
claims: Of the same incomplex thing there are two specifically distinct cognitions, intuitive and abstractive.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e1804.summary: Distinguishes two senses of abstractive cognition. (1) Cognition of something abstracted from many singulars, a universal. If the universal is a real quality in the soul (a probable view), it can be seen intuitively, and the same cognition is intuitive and abstractive in this sense. (2) Cognition abstracting from existence and non-existence and other contingent conditions, not knowing anything different from intuition but differing in mode. Intuitive cognition is that by which one can know whether a thing exists, so that if it exists the intellect at once judges that it exists, unless impeded by the cognition's imperfection. If God conserved a perfect intuition of a non-existent thing, the intellect would evidently know that it does not exist. Intuition likewise enables knowing whether one thing inheres in another, is distant from it, and other contingent truths, especially about the present. Abstractive cognition is that by which one cannot evidently know whether a contingent thing exists. All complex knowledge reduces to incomplex knowledge, so there must be an intuitive cognition from which experiential knowledge begins. As scientific knowledge of sensibles begins with sensitive intuition (Metaphysics I, Posterior Analytics II), so scientific knowledge of purely intelligibles begins with intellectual intuition. Through imperfection or obscurity of the intuition, or impediments in object or power, few or no contingent truths may be knowable from it.
claims: 'Abstractive' can mean cognition of a universal, or cognition abstracting from existence and non-existence.
If universals are qualities in the soul, they can be intuited.
Intuitive cognition is that by which one can evidently know whether a thing exists.
A divinely conserved intuition of a non-existent would yield knowledge that it does not exist.
Abstractive cognition does not enable evident knowledge of contingent existence.
Experiential and scientific knowledge begins from intuitive cognition.
Imperfect intuitions may yield few contingent truths.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e1973.summary: Draws consequences rejecting others' accounts. First, intuitive and abstractive cognition do not differ in that abstractive can be of existent or non-existent, present or absent, while intuitive is only of the present and really existent.
claims: Intuitive cognition is not restricted to present and existing objects.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e1987.summary: Second, they do not differ in that abstractive attains the object only under a diminished likeness and intuitive under its perfect ratio, as a certain doctor (Scotus, Quodlibet q.6) says.
claims: Abstractive cognition does not attain the object only by a diminished likeness.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e1998.summary: Third, they do not differ by formal moving rationes, as if in intuition the thing in its own existence moves per se, while in abstraction something else moves in which the thing has cognizable being, a cause virtually containing it or an effect such as a species (Scotus, Quodlibet q.13).
claims: Intuitive and abstractive cognition do not differ by what moves the intellect.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e2018.summary: Fourth, they do not differ in that intuitive cognition necessarily has a real actual relation to the object as present in its own existence, while abstractive has only a potential relation of measurability and dependence, not of union and presence (Scotus).
claims: Intuitive cognition does not necessarily involve a real relation to an existing object.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e2034.summary: Fifth, they do not differ in that in intuition the object is present in its own existence, while in abstraction it is present in something perfectly representing it (Scotus, Quodlibet q.3 and Book III d.10).
claims: Intuition does not require the object's presence in its own existence.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e2045.summary: Proves the first point from Scotus's own principles, which Ockham accepts here. In Book III d.9 Scotus proves that no form necessarily precedes vision: if it did, it would be an efficient cause, which God could replace (whatever God does through a mediate efficient cause he can do immediately), or a material cause. Likewise the existing present thing relates to intuition as efficient, material, formal or final cause. If efficient, God can produce the intuition without it.
claims: Whatever God does through a secondary efficient cause he can do immediately.
An existing object is at most an efficient cause of intuition, replaceable by God.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e2087.summary: Not material, since then with the thing existing and the intellect destroyed the thing could receive the cognition, and plainly intuition is not in the intuited thing as subject. Not formal, and not final, since any cognition can exist without any end except the first, as nothing requires a secondary end any more than a secondary efficient cause. Against 'the object is required as terminating object': either as terminating it is an essential cause, and the same argument applies, or it is not, and then, since every effect depends sufficiently on its essential causes, the intuition can exist with the object wholly destroyed. So intuition per se and necessarily is no more of the existent than of the non-existent. Abstractive cognition concerns neither existence nor non-existence, since no judgment of existence can be had through it.
claims: The object is not a material, formal or final cause of intuition.
An effect can exist given all its essential causes, with everything else removed.
Intuitive cognition can exist with its object destroyed.
Intuition per se concerns existence and non-existence equally.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e2143.summary: Proves the second point: the same thing under the same ratio is the object of intuition and abstraction. Among lower things there is nothing, and no proper ratio, under which a thing can be intuited without the intellect being able to doubt whether it exists when it is known, and so know it abstractively. Whatever real thing can be known abstractively can be known intuitively. On their own view, deity under the ratio of deity, God's most perfect ratio, can be known abstractively, and existence itself can be known abstractively.
claims: The same object under the same ratio is the object of both intuition and abstraction.
Whatever can be known abstractively can be known intuitively.
Existence itself can be known abstractively.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e2174.summary: Proves the third point: God can cause both cognitions through exactly the same, and the thing need not move objectively in its own existence, as shown.
claims: God can cause both cognitions through the same cause.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e2185.summary: Proves the fourth point: on their view a real relation cannot terminate at a non-being, but the object of intuition can be a non-being.
claims: A real relation cannot terminate at a non-being.
The object of intuition can be non-existent.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e2194.summary: Proves the fifth point: intuition does not require the thing to be present in its own existence, as shown.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e2207.summary: Ockham's view: intuitive and abstractive cognition differ by themselves, not by objects or causes, though naturally intuition cannot exist without the thing's existence, which is a mediate or immediate efficient cause of it. Abstractive cognition can naturally exist with the thing wholly destroyed. If the proponent of the rejected differences meant this, he has some truth about this cognition, though not in other matters to be discussed elsewhere.
claims: Intuitive and abstractive cognition differ intrinsically, not by objects or causes.
Naturally, intuition requires the thing's existence as an efficient cause.
Abstractive cognition can naturally exist with the thing destroyed.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e2233.summary: It follows that intuitive cognition, sensitive and intellectual, can be of a non-existent. Another proof: every absolute thing distinct in place and subject from another can exist by divine power without it, since it is implausible that if God wants to destroy something in heaven he must destroy something on earth. An intuitive vision, sensitive or intellectual, of a star in heaven is an absolute thing distinct in place and subject from the star, so the vision can remain when the star is destroyed.
claims: Intuitive cognition can be of a non-existent object.
Any absolute thing distinct in place and subject from another can exist without it by divine power.
A vision of a star can remain if God destroys the star.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e2267.summary: It also follows that God has intuitive cognition of all things, existing or not, since he knows creatures not to be when they are not, just as he knows them to be when they are.
claims: God has intuitive cognition of all things, existent or non-existent.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e2278.summary: Also, a non-existent thing can be intuitively known even though the object of the act does not exist, contrary to others: a sensitive vision of color can be conserved by God without the color, and still terminates at the color as first object. The same holds of intellectual intuition.
claims: A conserved vision terminates at its object even if the object does not exist.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e2294.summary: Also, our intellect in this state knows not only sensibles but also, particularly and intuitively, some intelligibles that fall under no sense, such as intellections, acts of will, pleasure and sorrow, which one experiences in oneself. 'I understand' is evident to me. If it is first and taken from incomplex knowledge, then, being contingent, some term or thing must be seen intuitively, since abstractive cognition abstracts from here and now, and intuition of the external thing alone does not suffice, so intuition of the intellection is required. It cannot be known through another prior contingent, since nothing entails 'I understand', and, given the will's freedom, nothing entails 'I love Socrates', not even 'I know Socrates is good' or 'I know Socrates should be loved', since the will can freely will against the intellect's dictate. So such propositions are first among contingents.
claims: In this state we intuitively know our own mental acts.
'I understand' is evidently known through intuition of the intellection.
Because of the will's freedom, nothing entails 'I love Socrates'.
The will can freely will against the intellect's dictate.
Propositions about one's own mental acts are first among contingents.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e2375.summary: Further: experiential knowledge cannot exist without intuition, and we gain science of these mental acts by experience, experiencing them in ourselves as we do sensibles, no more doubting that we love than that we are warmed. Augustine (De Trinitate XIII.1) confirms: faith in absent things is present, faith in external things is internal, faith in unseen things is within. So though the thing believed is known only abstractively, the faith by which it is believed is seen.
claims: Experiential knowledge requires intuitive cognition.
We experience our mental acts with the same certainty as sensible states.
Faith itself is seen while its object is known abstractively.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e2409.summary: Against the reply that Augustine speaks of supernatural things known only in a general concept: for him the thing and the faith are known differently, so if the thing is known in general, the faith must be known in particular. Also, as one can have faith about supernatural things, one can about particulars previously sensed and now absent. Then the faith concerns absent particulars once seen, which are known abstractively while the faith is known intuitively.
claims: Faith in previously sensed but now absent particulars is known intuitively while its objects are known abstractively.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e2435.summary: Augustine (De Trinitate XIII.2) also proves that faith belongs to no bodily sense: it is a matter of the heart, within us, and each sees it in himself, believing it to exist in others without seeing it. So one has intuitive knowledge of one's own faith, by which one evidently knows it exists, and abstractive knowledge of another's, by which one does not know whether it exists.
claims: One has intuitive knowledge of one's own faith and abstractive knowledge of another's.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e2458.summary: Objection: the difference is only that one's own faith is known in particular and another's only in general.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e2465.summary: Reply: true, we cannot now see or understand another's faith except by a common concept. But even if we understood another's faith in particular, as I understand a color previously seen, I could still doubt whether they believe, as I do not know whether that color still exists. So I would have specifically different cognitions of their faith and mine: if of the same species, I could see their faith as I see mine, since causes of the same kind have effects of the same kind. Augustine says the same of the will (De Trinitate XIII.3): seeing one's own will differs from seeing another's, which one may conjecture, as he is as certain of Rome's founding as of Constantinople though he saw only the latter. So of spiritual as of bodily things there is a cognition by which contingent truth can be known and one by which it cannot, and both are intellectual.
claims: Even particular knowledge of another's faith would not show whether it exists.
Knowledge of one's own and others' mental states differs in species.
Of spiritual things there are both intuitive and abstractive intellectual cognitions.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e2526.summary: Further: the contingent truths the intellect knows most certainly have terms most known intuitively in particular, since knowledge of contingent truth presupposes intuition in particular. Contingent truths about purely intelligible things are known most certainly, as experience and Augustine (De Trinitate XV) show: we may doubt sensibles, but not 'I know that I live', 'I want to be happy', 'I do not want to err'. Augustine says the mind perceives two kinds of things: those through bodily senses, against which the Academics argued, and others perceived through itself most firmly, such as 'I know I live', which they cannot doubt. So the intellect understands some things not previously sensed, and contingent truths about pure intelligibles are evident, presuppose no others, and require intuitive cognition of something purely intelligible. Lest this view be dismissed as new, he will cite an authority.
claims: Contingent truths about one's own mental life are the most certain contingent truths.
Such truths presuppose no other truths and require intellectual intuition.
Unlike sensible truths, they cannot be doubted by the skeptic.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e2607.summary: Cites the Subtle Doctor (Scotus, Book III d.45 q.3), who expressly holds both conclusions: the intellect intuitively knows sensibles and purely intelligibles. Since the intellect has a properly so-called act of remembering, it intuitively grasps the act it later remembers as its proximate object. The quotation follows.
claims: Scotus holds that the intellect intuitively knows sensibles and purely intelligible acts.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e2636.summary: Quotes Scotus at length: the intellective part has memory and a proper act of remembering. The intellect knows not only universals (true of abstractive intellection, which alone is scientific) but also intuitively what sense knows, since a higher power knows what a lower does, and it knows sensations. Both are shown by its knowing true contingent propositions and syllogizing from them, which is proper to the intellect, and their truth concerns objects intuitively known under the ratio of existence. So the intellect can perceive time, remember any object sense memory can, and also remember past intellections and volitions, which no sense can. Otherwise we could not prudently repent of bad volitions or order present speculation to what follows. Some remembering is proper to the intellect by both proximate and remote object, such as remembering that a triangle has three angles. Some is proper by proximate object yet could belong to sense, as remembering that I saw white.
claims: The intellect has its own memory and act of remembering (Scotus).
The intellect intuitively knows what sense knows and knows sensations (Scotus).
Remembering past intellections and volitions is proper to the intellect (Scotus).
Without intellectual memory, prudent repentance would be impossible (Scotus).

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e2764.summary: So Scotus holds, in substance and in words, that the intellect intuitively knows sensibles and some purely intelligibles. Against the reply that he speaks of the separated soul, he clearly also means this present state, since he speaks of a soul that can repent, order itself to further speculation, and remember sensations, which belong to the soul in this state.
claims: Scotus's claims concern the soul in this present state.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e2787.summary: If Scotus says the opposite elsewhere, Ockham is little moved: he cites him not as an authority and holds the view not because Scotus holds it but because he thinks it true. Still, since Scotus held it, his followers should not dismiss it as new.
claims: Ockham holds the view because it is true, not because of authority.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e2803.summary: Second article: by his absolute power God can be known by such a twofold cognition, intuitive and abstractive. This is hard to prove but can be argued. If God could not be known abstractively, it would be because of his identity with his existence, because he cannot be apprehended without being known to exist actually, or because an imperfect cognition cannot terminate at him. The first is no obstacle, since existence itself can be known abstractively. Nor the second, since one might doubt that the thing exists and know it only by discourse; even if an angel cannot doubt that it exists, it can know itself abstractively, as another angel can know it, and so God can be known abstractively though one cannot doubt that God exists. Nor the third, since an imperfect cognition in an imperfect power places no imperfection in the object.
claims: By absolute power God can be known both intuitively and abstractively.
God's identity with his existence does not prevent abstractive cognition.
An angel can know itself abstractively.
An imperfect cognition places no imperfection in its object.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e2845.summary: Further: all incomplex intelligibles can be known by similar cognitions, so as a creature can be known intuitively and abstractively, so can God.
claims: All incomplex intelligibles admit intuitive and abstractive cognition.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e2854.summary: Third article: each of these cognitions of God is separable from the other. They have no more essential or closer connection with respect to one object than another, and for creatures they are separable. Also, if abstractive cognition of God could not exist without intuitive, intuitive would be an essential cause of it, but it would only be an extrinsic one, and whatever God can do through an extrinsic cause he can do immediately.
claims: Intuitive and abstractive cognition of God are mutually separable.
Whatever God can do through an extrinsic cause he can do immediately.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e2880.summary: Fourth: distinct cognition of God is communicable to the wayfarer while remaining a wayfarer, since only intuitive cognition is incompatible with being a wayfarer. If abstractive cognition can exist without intuitive, distinct abstractive cognition of deity can exist in a wayfarer.
claims: Distinct abstractive cognition of deity is possible for a wayfarer.
Only intuitive cognition of God is incompatible with the wayfarer's state.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e2900.summary: Fifth, on the form of the question: by his absolute power God can cause in the wayfarer's intellect evident knowledge of some theological truths, and perhaps not of others.
claims: By absolute power God can cause evident knowledge of some theological truths in a wayfarer.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e2910.summary: To understand this: on one opinion, some predicates of God are true extramental things, since whatever the intellect understands by simple cognition it can compose with another or itself, saying 'this is this'.
claims: On one opinion things themselves can be predicated in mental propositions.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e2923.summary: Other predicates of God are only concepts with objective being, which on one opinion can truly be predicated of God, not for themselves but for the thing. These are simply absolute, connotative, or (on others' view) respective. Examples: in such an intellect 'Father' predicated of God or 'paternity is God' (a thing, if things can be predicated); 'God is a being', 'God is intellect' (absolute concepts); 'God is creator' or 'creative' (connotative).
claims: Concepts with objective being can be predicated of God for God.
Concepts predicated of God are absolute, connotative or respective.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e2945.summary: Second: some theological truths are merely contingent, such as 'God creates', 'God beatifies', 'God is incarnate'.
claims: Some theological truths are contingent.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e2954.summary: Others are necessary. Some of these have connotative predicates ('God is incarnable', 'God is creative'); others have non-connotative predicates, either things or univocal or connotative concepts.
claims: Necessary theological truths have either connotative or non-connotative predicates.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e2965.summary: Answers. First, no contingent proposition can be evidently known except from intuitive cognition of some extreme or what it signifies. If a contingent truth cannot be evidently known from intuitive cognition of a creature but presupposes intuitive cognition of deity, a wayfarer cannot evidently know it. So 'God is incarnate' cannot be evidently known from intuition of the human nature; it needs intuition of deity, and however distinctly one knew deity abstractively, one could not evidently know that God is incarnate. Likewise future contingents such as 'the resurrection of the dead will occur' and 'the blessed soul will be beatified forever' cannot be known evidently by a wayfarer. Whether one who intuits the divine essence could know them is doubtful. Second, necessary truths with connotative predicates whose evident knowledge depends on that of a contingent truth unknowable to a wayfarer cannot be evidently known by distinct abstractive cognition of deity; perhaps 'God is incarnable' is such. How this dependence works is treated in the next question. Third, necessary truths predicating a thing or a simply absolute concept are evidently knowable by such cognition. If a thing is predicated, it can only be something really God, so an intellect distinctly understanding deity evidently knows 'this thing is this'. If a concept is predicated, it must be univocal to God and others, and so known as one who knows whiteness knows that whiteness is a color.
claims: No contingent proposition is evidently known except from intuitive cognition of some extreme.
A wayfarer cannot evidently know that God is incarnate.
Future contingents about resurrection and beatitude cannot be evidently known by a wayfarer.
Necessary truths depending on unknowable contingents, like 'God is incarnable', may not be evidently knowable.
Necessary truths predicating things or absolute univocal concepts of God are evidently knowable through distinct abstractive cognition of deity.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e3063.summary: Sixth: raises doubts. First doubt, about apprehensive and judicative acts: they do not seem compatible in one intellect, since one cannot apprehend a proposition without assenting, dissenting or doubting, so there is no act about a complex beyond these.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e3082.summary: Second doubt: how incomplex knowledge of terms, apprehension of the complex, and the following judgment relate, whether all are really distinct, and whether each can exist without the others.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e3093.summary: Third doubt, about the first article: there seems not to be a twofold cognition. Some argue that one power cannot have specifically distinct acts about one object under one ratio. Acts depend essentially only on power or object; one agent and one matter give one effect (Metaphysics VIII); the same as such always makes the same (De generatione II); acts are distinguished by objects (De anima II). Also, the intellect seems not to have intuitive cognition, since intuition concerns only singulars, while the intellect understands only universals and abstracts from here and now.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e3130.summary: Fourth doubt: what intuitive cognition in this state concerns, suggesting only sensibles. Acts of understanding are intelligible only reflexively, while intuition is direct. And there would be infinitely many simultaneous intellections: if the first is intuited because sufficiently present, the intuition of it is equally present and would be intuited by a third, and so on infinitely.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e3159.summary: Against the reply that one could go on infinitely but there are not in fact infinitely many: a total natural cause sufficiently near a disposed patient, not acting in time, produces its effect at once. The second intellection with the power is the total cause of the third, so the third exists at once, and so on infinitely. Aristotle (De anima III) also says one who does not sense learns nothing and must contemplate with phantasms, and Averroes (comm. 39) says the intellect understands nothing in particular except the singular sense apprehends.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e3205.summary: Further, from On Memory and Recollection: there is no understanding without a phantasm.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e3210.summary: Further, from On Sense: nothing is in the intellect that was not first in sense.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e3216.summary: Further: what is intuitively known is perfectly known, so it could be known as distinct from everything else intuitively known. Then one could evidently know whether direct and reflexive acts, or love and delight, are really distinct, which are doubtful.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e3232.summary: Fifth doubt: whether intuitive cognition concerns habits as well as acts, since habits are as present as acts.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e3243.summary: Sixth doubt: whether intuitive cognition and the judgment that a thing exists or not are really distinct. Not identical, since nothing can be really identical with two opposites, and while the same intuition remains unchanged, the intellect judges the thing to exist when it does and not when it does not, so neither judgment is the intuition.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e3263.summary: Likewise, if the intellect intuited whiteness and its subject with one unchanged vision, and God then separated them, it would judge first 'this is white' and then 'this is not white', having opposite judgments compatible with one intuition. So neither judgment is identical with it.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e3281.summary: Nor can they be really distinct. First, since the intuition is prior, God could make it without the judgment, so one could intuit an existing thing perfectly and not know whether it exists, and could love without knowing one loves, against Augustine. Second, one could intuit an existing thing and judge that it does not exist: when an absolute thing is compatible with and separable from another, its absolute opposite is compatible too (the same subject receives contraries), so if the judgment of existence is separable from the intuition, the opposite judgment could coexist with it.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e3327.summary: Seventh doubt: how intuition of a non-existent could yield evident knowledge that it does not exist. What causes the judgment? Not the intellective power, which is unchanged whether or not the thing exists and, being a natural cause, cannot produce opposite effects in the same patient. Not the intuition alone, for the same reason. Not the intuited thing, which simply does not exist and so causes nothing.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e3361.summary: Eighth doubt: intuitive cognition seems unable to be of a non-existent, since then God could beatify an intellect by intuition even if God did not exist.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e3372.summary: Likewise, a creature could then delight as much in the absence of the delightful as in its presence, since delight can be sufficiently posited given intuitive cognition of the thing.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e3381.summary: Ninth doubt: about God being distinctly known abstractively. God is present either in himself, in which case the cognition is intuitive, being of something really present, or in something else, which is either known or only a ratio cognoscendi. Not the former, since nothing other than God leads to distinct knowledge of deity. Not the latter, since nothing other than God, infinitely less perfect, distinctly represents God under the ratio of deity.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e3403.summary: Tenth doubt: that such cognition is communicable to the wayfarer, since all abstractive cognition of a thing presupposes intuitive cognition of it, and intuition of God is not communicable.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e3416.summary: Answers the first doubt: the apprehensive act is really distinct from acts of assenting, dissenting and doubting and compatible with each, though perhaps it cannot naturally occur without one of them. So whoever apprehends a proposition assents, dissents or doubts, yet apprehension is distinct from each. Proof: if someone often doubts a complex, so that a habit inclines them to think of it, and later assents for some principle or authority, they then apprehend and assent more readily than if they had never doubted. Something acquired during the doubting inclines to assent, and it cannot be the habit of doubting, which would incline away from assent. So another habit was acquired with it, and as habits differ, so do the acts generating them.
claims: The apprehensive act is really distinct from assent, dissent and doubt.
Apprehension may not naturally occur without one of them.
Doubting a proposition can facilitate later assent through an apprehensive habit.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e3492.summary: Answers the second doubt: it can probably be said that incomplex knowledge of terms, apprehension of the complex, and the following judgment differ really, and each is separable from the others by divine power. The first was shown. The second: separability by divine power should be denied of no absolute thing really distinct from another unless an evident contradiction appears, and none appears in a judgment without apprehension or an apprehension without incomplex knowledge of terms.
claims: Incomplex knowledge, apprehension and judgment are really distinct.
Each is separable from the others by divine power.
Separability by divine power should be denied only given an evident contradiction.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e3519.summary: Against the claim that assent without apprehension or apprehension of a complex without apprehension of its terms is an evident contradiction: it is not contradictory that an intellect assent without an apprehension really distinct from the assent, though assenting without any apprehension is, since assent is itself a kind of apprehension, besides the other one. Similarly one can apprehend a complex without incomplex knowledge of the terms, while having complex knowledge by which complex and terms are known. If both cognitions of the terms coexist, this can be granted, since the incomplex cognition has no repugnance to the complex one, and without evident experience that it is destroyed it should not be denied to remain. They differ in species, and distinct acts in one power about one object are not unfitting.
claims: Assent is itself a kind of apprehension.
Terms can be known both in complex and incomplex cognitions at once.
A cognition should not be held destroyed without evident experience.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e3580.summary: Whatever holds by absolute power, naturally the first is separable from the two following and the second from the third, but the third is in no way separable from the two preceding, nor the second from the first. One reason: whenever an apprehensive or judicative act is elicited, an act about the terms is too, generating a habit, so no act is elicited through those habits without the habit of the terms also inclining. Those who deny that every absolute thing is separable from every other, as is commonly held that volition cannot exist without cognition, can as easily say that apprehension cannot exist without incomplex knowledge, nor judgment without both. Answers the third doubt: there can be two specifically distinct cognitions of the same object under the same ratio.
claims: Naturally, judgment cannot exist without apprehension and incomplex knowledge.
Volition cannot naturally exist without cognition.
Two specifically distinct cognitions of one object under one ratio are possible.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e3628.summary: To the argument to the contrary: in one power there can be such distinct cognitions of one object.
claims: One power can have distinct cognitions of one object.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e3635.summary: To the first proof: these cognitions are distinguished formally by themselves, and causally by the essential causes from which they have being, though they need not require distinct essential causes, since one simple cause such as God can produce many. So they depend essentially on something besides object and power. Naturally, though, they have distinct effective causes: the immediate effective cause of intuition is the known thing itself, while that of abstraction is the intuition itself or another habit inclining to abstraction. Even if acts depended essentially only on object and power, they could still differ specifically, since one wholly or relatively unlimited agent can produce specifically distinct effects in the same patient. So one agent and one matter can have several specifically distinct effects.
claims: Intuitive and abstractive cognitions are distinguished by themselves.
Naturally, the known thing causes intuition and intuition (or a habit) causes abstraction.
An unlimited agent can produce specifically distinct effects in one patient.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e3679.summary: Aristotle and the Commentator speak of a natural sufficient agent and incompatible forms, like those of chest and bench, as the Commentator's example shows. Their intent will be discussed elsewhere.
claims: The principle 'one agent, one effect' concerns natural agents and incompatible forms.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e3692.summary: To the third proof: in De generatione II Aristotle speaks of a natural agent that, remaining the same, always does the same: what it does at one time it does at another, absent variation in patient, agent or impediment. It need not do precisely one thing: the sun by the same power produces heat and light in the medium, always the same yet many.
claims: A natural agent always does the same, but that may include many effects.
The sun produces both heat and light by the same power.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e3728.summary: To the fourth proof: acts are distinguished by objects, since from distinct objects, one apprehended by an act and not another, follows specific distinction of acts. But identity of objects does not entail identity of acts: if a is the object of an intellection and b of a volition, and a and b are simply one, the intellection of a and the volition of b are not one act. So even with the same object, abstractive and intuitive cognition differ.
claims: Distinct objects imply distinct acts, but the same object does not imply the same act.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e3754.summary: This answers De anima III, that sciences are divided as things are: diversity of knowables entails diversity of sciences, yet of the same complex there can be specifically distinct acts, since per Posterior Analytics I there can be science and opinion, or error and science, about the same conclusion, and erring and knowing differ in species.
claims: Science, opinion and error can concern the same conclusion and differ in species.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e3774.summary: Notes that although distinct knowables can have distinct sciences, one habit can be equivalent to, or equivalently contain, several habits of propositions or knowables, so that neither is its total object, only partial, as one complex cognition has both terms as partial objects.
claims: One habit can equivalently contain several habits with partial objects.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e3794.summary: To the argument that the intellect lacks intuition because it does not know singulars: in this state the intellect knows the singular, and first, as first known by primacy of generation. Aristotle does not deny this but holds that the intellect understands universals and sense singulars, statements he writes to mark the difference between intellect and sense. That difference holds if the intellect knows universals as well as singulars while sense knows only singulars, so it does not prevent the intellect knowing the singular first, though not exclusively.
claims: In this state the intellect knows the singular first, by primacy of generation.
Intellect differs from sense by also knowing universals.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e3829.summary: To the argument from abstraction from here and now: the intellect does not abstract from here and now in every intellection. It has an abstractive cognition by which it cannot judge here and now, like imagination, and another, intuitive, by which it can judge that something is here and now, as the senses can. Abstraction from matter and material conditions is not on the object's side in every intellection, since in this state the very same thing under the same ratio is the first object of external sense and intellect by primacy of generation. Afterwards the intellect can abstract and form common concepts, which sense cannot. Taken universally, the abstraction is on the side of the intellection, which is immaterial, unlike sensation.
claims: The intellect does not abstract from here and now in every act.
The first object of intellect and external sense is the same in this state.
The intellect later forms common concepts by abstraction.
Intellection is immaterial, unlike sensation.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e3897.summary: Answers the fourth doubt: as proved, our intellect in this state understands some purely intelligible things particularly and intuitively.
claims: In this state we intuitively know purely intelligible items.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e3907.summary: To the first contrary argument: strictly, no intellection is reflexive, since strict reflection requires at least two items, as in reflected local motion.
claims: Strictly speaking no intellection is reflexive.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e3918.summary: Taking reflection broadly, such intellection is reflexive yet intuitive, as an angel can understand itself intuitively as well as another, and in doing so has a broadly reflexive intellection.
claims: Broadly reflexive intellection can be intuitive.
An angel can intuit itself.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e3931.summary: To the regress argument: it tells against every opinion, since if I know something I can know that I know it, and that I know that, and so on (Augustine, De Trinitate XV). The same question arises for abstractive cognition. So one must stop at the first intellection, which is intuited, and in this state that intellection impedes a second intuition. Not simply, but because its presence is not sufficient for a second intellection. The reason can only be the nature of things, known by experience, since these intellections do not conflict. On the authorities: Aristotle and the Commentator speak of the first intellection by primacy of generation, since in this state nothing is understood first except the sensible. Hence the Commentator says the intellection is the same as what sense apprehends, or he speaks of what is abstracted from what is first understood, namely sensibles.
claims: The regress objection applies to every theory of self-knowledge.
One must stop at the first intuited intellection.
In this state the presence of an intellection does not suffice for a further intuition of it.
The reason is the nature of things, known by experience.
In this state the first thing understood is the sensible.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e4014.summary: To On Memory: nothing is understood without a phantasm, because in this state all intellectual cognition presupposes sensitive imagination of external or internal sense. Against 'intuition is first, so it presupposes no other': it presupposes no other cognition of the same object in the same power, but does presuppose cognition in another power. Intellectual intuition of whiteness presupposes sensitive cognition of it, and intuition of an intellection, affection or delight presupposes cognition of its object. If love without prior cognition were possible, intuition of it would presuppose nothing, but that is impossible in this state. To On Sense: Aristotle means not that nothing is understood unless first in sense, but that no external sensible is understood unless first under sense. The mind does not intuit external things without prior sensitive intuition of them, but it can intuit internal things such as acts of intellect, will and delight without sensitive cognition of them, though sensitive cognition of some things is presupposed.
claims: In this state all intellectual cognition presupposes sensitive imagination.
Intellectual intuition presupposes cognition in another power, not in the same power.
'Nothing in the intellect not first in sense' concerns external sensibles only.
The mind intuits its own acts without sensitive intuition of them.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e4092.summary: To the last argument: perhaps what is intuited clearly and perfectly can be discerned from anything specifically distinct and intuited clearly and perfectly, but not what is intuited obscurely and imperfectly. In this state our intellect intuits nothing clearly and perfectly, so it cannot discern direct from reflexive acts and the like, though it can discern some things. Augustine seems to agree (De Trinitate X.4, X.18): the mind can perceive itself yet not discern itself from other things.
claims: In this state our intuitions are obscure and imperfect.
Obscure intuition does not allow discrimination of specifically distinct objects.
The mind can perceive itself without discerning itself from other things (Augustine).

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e4136.summary: Answers the fifth doubt: in this state intuition does not extend to all intelligibles equally present. It concerns acts, not habits, as experience shows: everyone experiences loving and delighting, but not being inclined by a habit, since God acting could incline the power as much as a habit. So the experienced inclination does not evidently reveal a habit by intuition, which can be known only by reasoning. So no one can intuitively see faith and charity, which are habits in us, though the acts they elicit, believing and loving, can be intuited.
claims: In this state we intuit our acts but not our habits.
Habits are known only by reasoning, not intuition.
God could produce the same inclination as a habit.
Faith and charity as habits cannot be intuited; believing and loving can.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e4174.summary: Answers the sixth doubt: intuitive cognition and the judgment are really distinct, since intuition concerns an incomplex and judgment a complex. The 'judgment' following sensitive intuition alone is not distinct from it, nor is an intellectual judgment resting in incomplex knowledge alone. It is not properly a judgment, since it does not concern a complex, but only an equivalent judgment.
claims: Intuitive cognition and judgment are really distinct.
A sensitive 'judgment' is only an equivalent judgment, not distinct from the sensation.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e4198.summary: To the first contrary argument: the intuition can occur without the consequent judgment, so one can love and not judge that one loves, just as one can know the terms of a self-evident proposition, and even apprehend it, without knowing it.
claims: Intuition can exist without the consequent judgment.
One can love without judging that one loves.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e4216.summary: Against 'then it is not self-evident, since such a proposition is known once the terms are apprehended': a self-evident proposition is one for whose evident knowledge the terms suffice, with God's general influence. God can impede intuitive knowledge, but it suffices for evident knowledge that the thing exists, unless there is an impediment or the intuition's activity is impeded.
claims: A self-evident proposition is one whose terms suffice for evident knowledge, given God's general concurrence.
God can impede the effect of an intuition.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e4236.summary: To the second: it is not unfitting that a thing be intuitively seen while the intellect believes it does not exist, though this cannot happen naturally. For intuitive cognition it suffices that, of itself, it is sufficient to produce a correct judgment about the thing's existence or non-existence.
claims: By divine power one could intuit a thing and believe it does not exist.
Intuition of itself suffices for a correct judgment of existence.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e4249.summary: Answers the seventh doubt: through intuition of a thing one can evidently know that it does not exist when it does not. The judgment can be caused by the intuition. Against 'it would cause the opposite effect if the thing existed': a cause together with another partial cause can produce one effect, while alone it produces the opposite. So the proper intuition together with the thing causes the judgment that it exists, and the intuition without the thing causes the opposite judgment. The causes of these judgments are not the same: intuition without the thing, versus intuition with the thing as partial cause.
claims: Intuition of a non-existent can cause the judgment that it does not exist.
A cause with a partial co-cause can produce one effect and alone the opposite.
The thing itself is a partial cause of the judgment that it exists.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e4293.summary: Answers the eighth doubt: it is contradictory that God not exist and yet intuitive cognition of God exist, so it is no wonder that something unfitting follows.
claims: Intuitive cognition of God without God's existence is contradictory.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e4301.summary: To the next: it does not seem unfitting that by divine power delight be as great in absence as in presence. Augustine's example (De Trinitate) shows very great delight through abstractive cognition alone, so it could be greater through intuitive.
claims: By divine power delight could be as great in absence as in presence.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e4319.summary: Answers the ninth doubt: God is present in himself with the presence required for intuitive cognition, but it does not follow that the cognition is intuitive. If God could not exist, no presence in himself or in another would be required, just as God can now create cognition of a non-existent without any prior presence.
claims: God's presence does not make every cognition of him intuitive.
God can create cognition of a non-existent without any presence.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e4337.summary: Answers the last doubt: every abstractive cognition of anything naturally known presupposes intuitive cognition of it, because no intellect can naturally acquire knowledge of a thing except through the thing as partial efficient cause, and every cognition that by nature requires the thing's coexistence is intuitive. So the first cognition of a thing is intuitive. But God can cause abstractive cognition of deity and other things without prior intuition, and such abstractive cognition of deity is communicable to the wayfarer.
claims: Naturally, abstractive cognition presupposes intuitive cognition of the same thing.
The first natural cognition of a thing is intuitive.
God can cause abstractive cognition without prior intuition.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e4363.summary: Answers the first principal argument: distinct knowledge of deity under its proper ratio is possible for the wayfarer, but it is not beatific. Only intuitive knowledge of the infinite beatifying object is beatific, and only abstractive knowledge is possible for the wayfarer.
claims: Distinct knowledge of deity is possible for the wayfarer but is not beatific.
Only intuitive knowledge of God is beatific.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e4383.summary: Answers the second: some theological truths would be self-evident to such an intellect, others perhaps known through better-known ones. If it apprehended deity and the personal properties distinctly in themselves, 'deity is three persons' would be self-evident because of the persons' real identity with the essence, no more doubtable than 'God is deity'. Such an intellect could also form our proposition 'God is three persons', which would be evident but not self-evident, known through the first, from which it formally follows. They are distinct propositions because their terms differ: the first has things in themselves (or mental intentions the wayfarer cannot have), the second has the concepts we actually have, since we cannot distinctly know God or anything really God in itself. Whoever knows those terms evidently knows such propositions, but that is not possible for us under the common state. 'God is three and one' can be made known through a prior proposition, since the predicate belongs first to God in himself, or to an intention impossible for the wayfarer, before it belongs to the concept that is subject in our proposition.
claims: 'Deity is three persons' would be self-evident to an intellect knowing deity in itself.
Our 'God is three persons' would then be evident but not self-evident.
Propositions with different terms are distinct propositions.
We cannot distinctly know God in himself in the common state.

wo8uy7-d1e69-d1e4470.summary: Answers the third: granting that evident knowledge is most perfect in species, meaning no specifically distinct knowledge is as perfect, one evident knowledge can still be more perfect than another of the same species. The blessed's knowledge of a truth is more perfect than a non-blessed's because intuition of the terms causes more perfect knowledge than abstraction. Someone holding that intuitive and abstractive cognitions cause specifically distinct effects could say that evident knowledge caused by intuition of deity and the persons is more perfect and specifically distinct, so not every evident theological knowledge is most perfect. Against this is the principle that plurality is not to be posited without necessity: since specifically distinct causes can produce effects of the same species, no specific distinction should be posited among the complex cognitions they cause. A specific distinction would need some other reason, which is hard to find. This ends the first principal question.
claims: Evident knowledge of the same species can vary in perfection.
The blessed know theological truths more perfectly because of intuitive cognition of terms.
Plurality is not to be posited without necessity.
Complex cognitions caused by intuitive and abstractive cognition need not differ in species.

wo8uy7-d1e69.summary: Prologue question 1, the opening question of the commentary, asks whether the wayfarer's intellect can have evident knowledge of theological truths. Ockham defines the wayfarer as lacking intuitive cognition of God but able to attain it by ordained power. Evident knowledge is knowledge of a true complex apt to be caused by incomplex knowledge of terms, so it covers contingent truths too. Theological truths are those necessary for salvation, some naturally knowable. He argues that metaphysics and theology are aggregates of habits that can share truths. The core is his theory of cognition. He distinguishes apprehensive from judicative acts and habits, with judgment presupposing apprehension and incomplex knowledge, and no sensitive act as proximate cause of judgment. He argues that of the same object under the same ratio there are two specifically distinct incomplex cognitions: intuitive, by which one can evidently know whether a thing exists and other contingent facts, and abstractive, by which one cannot. Intellectual, not only sensitive, intuition of sensible singulars is required, and in this state we also intuit our own purely intelligible acts (understanding, loving, delighting, believing). This is supported by Augustine and, he notes, by Scotus himself. He rejects Scotus's criteria for distinguishing the cognitions (presence, diminished likeness, moving rationes, real relation) and holds that they differ intrinsically. Since intuition is an absolute thing separable from its object, God could conserve an intuition of a non-existent star, and it would yield the judgment that the star does not exist. Applying this to God, both cognitions of deity are possible by absolute power and are separable, so distinct abstractive cognition of God is communicable to a wayfarer. Hence God can cause evident knowledge of some theological truths in a wayfarer: necessary truths predicating things or absolute univocal concepts. Not contingent truths such as the Incarnation or future resurrection, which require intuition of deity, nor perhaps necessary truths that depend on them. Ten doubts are resolved, including the reality and separability of apprehension and judgment, the regress of reflexive intellection, the dependence of intellect on phantasms, the non-intuitability of habits like faith and charity, and the causation of judgments of non-existence. The question ends with an appeal to the principle of parsimony.
claims: By absolute power God can give a wayfarer evident knowledge of some theological truths.
There are specifically distinct intuitive and abstractive cognitions of the same object.
Intuitive cognition is that by which one can evidently know whether a thing exists.
There is intellectual intuition of sensible singulars and of one's own mental acts.
God could conserve an intuition of a non-existent, yielding the judgment that it does not exist.
Contingent theological truths like the Incarnation cannot be evidently known by a wayfarer.
Apprehension and judgment are really distinct acts.
Plurality is not to be posited without necessity.
